question: A main agent is configured with permission_mode="bypassPermissions" and spawns a subagent with a narrower, safety-focused system prompt to review untrusted code. What is the security implication of this setup?
options: A) The subagent's narrower system prompt overrides the inherited permission mode, effectively restricting it to only the tools its prompt mentions
B) The subagent automatically runs in default mode instead, since subagents always start with the most restrictive permission mode available regardless of the parent's setting
C) Permission mode has no effect on subagents at all, since subagents are sandboxed into a separate process with its own independent tool access
D) The subagent inherits bypassPermissions from the parent and cannot have that mode overridden per subagent, so it also gets full, autonomous system access despite its narrower prompt
correct_answers: D) The subagent inherits bypassPermissions from the parent and cannot have that mode overridden per subagent, so it also gets full, autonomous system access despite its narrower prompt
explanations: Incorrect. A system prompt shapes behavior and intent but does not restrict which tools are technically approved; the inherited permission mode still governs tool approval.
Incorrect. Subagents do not default to the most restrictive mode; they inherit the parent's mode when it is bypassPermissions, acceptEdits, or auto.
Incorrect. Subagents are not isolated from the parent's permission configuration; the documented behavior is inheritance of the parent's mode, not independence from it.

Correct. When the parent uses bypassPermissions, acceptEdits, or auto, subagents inherit that mode and it cannot be overridden per subagent, so a narrowly-prompted subagent still gets full autonomous access unless an explicit ask rule forces a prompt.
